5:7.text: Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.

provenance.other: “arise from the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:14; “awake out of sleep” occurs in exactly one, Romans 13:11. Both are Pauline and both belong to the same small figure — sleep, waking, and light — which the KJV has nowhere else in this combination. “deep sleep” by itself occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and is no help.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:7 puts four things in one sentence and Ephesians 5 puts the same four in four verses: sleep, waking, darkness, light. 'Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord' (5:8); 'Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light' (5:14). What the Book of Mormon adds is the object of the waking — 'they awoke unto God' — and the source of the light, 'the light of the everlasting word', which turns Paul's baptismal summons into a report of a conversion that has already happened. The metalepsis is in what Ephesians 5:14 is: a fragment the KJV marks as a citation ('Wherefore he saith'), a hymn quoted inside the epistle. Alma 5:7 is therefore quoting a quotation, and the awakening it describes is the one the church sings about itself.

5:7.note: 'He awaked them out of a deep sleep, and they awoke unto God. Behold, they were in the midst of darkness; nevertheless, their souls were illuminated by the light of the everlasting word.' Ephesians 5:14 is the KJV's one verse joining sleep to rising and to Christ giving light, and Romans 13:11-12 — 'to awake out of sleep ... the night is far spent, the day is at hand; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness' — supplies the waking verb and the darkness. Neither is reproduced as a clause; the case is the co-occurrence of the whole figure with two KJV singletons inside it.

5:15.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “this mortal must put on immortality” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “put on incorruption” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 15:53 and 15:54, which are the same sentence stated and then restated. No other KJV passage pairs mortal with immortality and corruption with incorruption.
provenance.significance: Two changes are worth recording. Paul's order is corruption first and mortality second; Alma's is mortality first and corruption second, so the Book of Mormon reverses the couplet while keeping both halves. And Paul's verb is 'put on' — a garment metaphor that governs the whole of 1 Corinthians 15:53-54 — where Alma 5:15 has 'raised'. That matters here because the garment metaphor is not lost, it is moved: six verses later, at 5:21-24, this sermon's whole argument turns on garments washed white and garments stained, and Paul's clothing of the resurrection body is where the KJV keeps that image. The chapter takes the doctrine in one verse and the metaphor in another.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 5:10's 'the things done in his body' stands behind the second half of Alma 5:15, 'judged according to the deeds which hath been done in the mortal body'; that link is adjudicated at 2 Nephi 9:15.

5:15.note: 'View this mortal body raised in immortality, and this corruption raised in incorruption.' Against 1 Corinthians 15:53: 'For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.' Both antitheses, both demonstratives, and the KJV's abstract nouns; only the verb and the order of the pair are changed. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations, and catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the two clauses are reproduced as clauses.

5:16.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “come ye blessed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has 'Come unto me ye blessed', which splices Matthew 25:34's greeting onto Matthew 11:28's invitation, a phrase this same sermon uses twice at 5:34 and 5:35.
provenance.significance: This is the second of three places where Alma's preaching runs on Matthew 25, and the three are in the parable's own order: the neglected at Alma 4:12 (the goats' list, Matthew 25:44), the welcome at 5:16 (Matthew 25:34), and the inheritance at the right hand at 5:58 (Matthew 25:33-34). Recovering the context sharpens Alma's question rather than merely sourcing it. In Matthew the sentence is spoken by the King to people who did not know they had served him — 'when saw we thee an hungred?' — whereas Alma asks his hearers to imagine hearing it said of works they can already name, 'your works have been the works of righteousness upon the face of the earth'. The next verse then withdraws the imagining as a possible lie. Matthew's sheep are surprised; Alma's audience is invited to audit itself in advance, which is a use of the parable the parable does not make.

5:16.note: 'Can you imagine to yourselves that ye hear the voice of the Lord, saying unto you, in that day, Come unto me ye blessed.' The greeting is the KJV's only 'come, ye blessed', at Matthew 25:34, with 'unto me' carried over from the other great invitation. Alma 4:12 has already borrowed from the far side of the same parable and 5:58 will borrow the right hand, so the row also fixes the recurrence.

5:19.text: He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.

provenance.other: “clean hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 24:4 and Job 17:9, and “a pure heart” in exactly four; the two are joined in one clause only at Psalm 24:4. Alma 5:19 inverts the order to 'a pure heart and clean hands'.
provenance.significance: Psalm 24 is an entrance liturgy: 'Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?' — and the answer is the man with clean hands and a pure heart. Alma 5:19 asks the same question about the same qualification and moves it to the judgment: 'can ye look up to God at that day with a pure heart and clean hands?' The gate the psalm guards is a temple gate in this life and Alma has made it the last one. The transposition is exact enough to be deliberate: both are entrance examinations, both turn on the same two possessions, and both are put as a question rather than a rule.

5:19.note: 'Can ye look up to God at that day with a pure heart and clean hands?' The pair is Psalm 24:4's and is joined nowhere else in the KJV. Note what the sermon does with it four verses on: the psalm's clean hands become garments washed white at 5:21-24, so the same test is put twice, once in the psalm's terms and once in Revelation's.

5:19.text: But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away:

provenance.other: “engraven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:7, and that verse also carries 'countenance' — the two words Alma 5:19 puts together. Alma 5:14's 'received his image in your countenances' supplies the third term, and 'image' is the governing noun of the same Pauline passage at 3:18.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 3 is the KJV's one place where engraving, a shining countenance, and being changed into an image belong to a single argument: the law was 'written and engraven in stones' and left Moses' face too bright to look at, whereas those who behold the Lord 'are changed into the same image from glory to glory'. Alma 5:14 and 5:19 ask a congregation whether that change has happened to their faces — 'have ye received his image in your countenances ... can you look up, having the image of God engraven upon your countenances?' Paul's contrast is between what is engraven in stone and what is written in the heart; Alma's question moves the engraving onto the face, which is the one surface Paul's argument leaves it off.
provenance.alternative: The image language may be Genesis 1:26-27's and the engraving simply a metaphor of permanence, in which case there is no contact with 2 Corinthians at all.

5:19.note: 'Can you look up, having the image of God engraven upon your countenances?' The interest is a lexical accident worth recording: the KJV inflects 'engrave' this way exactly once, and that once is in the passage where the glory of Moses' countenance is being argued against the changing of believers into an image. Two verses of Alma 5 supply all three of that passage's nouns.
5:19.whyNot: No clause is shared and the words arrive in different grammatical roles — Paul engraves a law in stones, Alma engraves an image on faces. 'Engraven' may simply be the natural KJV-register participle for a writer who has already used 'engraven' vocabulary of the plates elsewhere in the corpus, in which case the singleton is an artifact of English morphology rather than evidence of contact. Withdraw if a reader thinks 'image' and 'countenance' are independently available from Genesis 1:26.

5:21.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.other: “washed their robes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Revelation 7:14 is also the only KJV verse in which a garment is made white by blood, which is the paradox Alma 5:21 and 5:27 both state and neither explains.
provenance.significance: The image is impossible on its face — blood whitens nothing — and Revelation supplies the only warrant in the KJV for using it, so the borrowing is not decorative. What Alma does with it is to run it both ways at once: at 5:21 and 5:27 garments are made white through the blood of Christ, and at 5:22 garments are 'stained with blood' as the evidence that will testify the wearer a murderer. The same fluid cleanses and convicts within two verses, and the sermon relies on the reader hearing Revelation 7:14 under the first use to feel the second. Revelation 3:5 then supplies the next move: the one who overcomes is clothed in white raiment and his name is not blotted out of the book of life — which is exactly where this sermon goes at 5:57-58.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 1:5, 'washed us from our sins in his own blood', has the washing without the garments and may be the proximate phrase.

5:21.note: 'There can no man be saved except his garments are washed white; yea, his garments must be purified until they are cleansed from all stain, through the blood of him ... which should come to redeem his people from their sins.' The KJV washes robes once, at Revelation 7:14, and makes them white in blood once, in the same clause. Alma 5:24's 'whose garments are cleansed, and are spotless, pure and white' repeats it, as does 5:27; adjudicated here at first use.

5:21.text: And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.

provenance.other: “his people from their sins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has the clause entire with one verb changed, 'redeem' for 'save'; “redeem his people” occurs in no KJV verse at all. The formula is used three times in two chapters — Alma 5:21, 5:27 and 6:8 — and adjudicated here at first use.
provenance.significance: Matthew 1:21 is not a statement about atonement, it is an etymology: 'thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.' The clause exists in the KJV to explain a name. That is what makes its arrival in Alma 5 worth recording, because the sermon's central demand, eleven verses later, is precisely about a name — 'in his own name he doth call you, which is the name of Christ ... if ye will not hearken unto the voice of the good shepherd, to the name by which ye are called' (5:38). Alma 5:21 supplies the definition of the name and 5:38 asks whether the hearers answer to it. The substitution of 'redeem' for 'save' is the Book of Mormon's own and shifts the clause from naming to purchase, which is also the direction 5:27's blood and 5:42's wages are moving.

5:21.note: 'Through the blood of him of whom it hath been spoken by our fathers which should come to redeem his people from their sins.' Five words reproduced exactly from the KJV's one verse that has them, with the governing verb replaced. The machine ranked Matthew 1:21 at both 5:21 and 5:27 and was right, which is worth saying because it was right for the usual wrong reason — the run is long — and the evidence that makes it a link is that the run is unique.

5:24.text: There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when ye shall see Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, and you yourselves thrust out.

provenance.route: Luke 13:28-29, with Matthew 8:11-12 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sit down in the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 13:29; “children of the kingdom” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 8:12 and Matthew 13:38. The saying exists in two Gospel forms and Alma 5:24-25 has elements only one of them supplies: Luke names 'all the prophets' beside the patriarchs and says 'kingdom of God', which is Alma's wording, while Matthew names the patriarchs without prophets and says 'kingdom of heaven'. A third element comes from neither Gospel: “with Abraham with Isaac and with Jacob”, with the preposition repeated before each name, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 2:24 — 'God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.' Matthew 8:11 and Luke 13:28 both read 'with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob'. Alma 5:24 has the Exodus form of the list inside the Gospel form of the saying.
provenance.significance: The two verses take the two halves of one saying and keep them in the saying's own order. Luke 13:28-29 gives the seating — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, with those who are thrust out watching — and Alma 5:24 reproduces the list with 'all the holy prophets' in Luke's slot. Matthew 8:12 then gives the sentence Alma 5:25 needs and Luke does not have: 'the children of the kingdom shall be cast out.' Alma turns that phrase inside out. In Matthew the children of the kingdom are the ones expelled from it; in Alma they are expelled and reassigned — 'they are the children of the kingdom of the Devil' — so the paradox Matthew leaves standing, that the kingdom's own children lose it, is resolved by giving them another kingdom to be children of. The patriarch formula itself is worth the extra line. The repeated preposition is the Pentateuch's covenant idiom and its one KJV instance, Exodus 2:24, is the verse where God remembers the covenant and the exodus begins — so the list Alma uses to describe who sits down in the kingdom is worded as the list of those to whom a promise was made, not as the list of dinner guests the Gospels give.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 8:11 alone, if 'all the holy prophets' is thought to be the Book of Mormon's own addition rather than Luke's contribution; the phrase is a standing formula elsewhere in the corpus.

5:24.note: 'Do ye suppose that such an one can have a place to sit down in the Kingdom of God, with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob, and also all the holy prophets ... they shall be cast out, for they are the children of the kingdom of the Devil.' The seating is Luke's — his is the only KJV verse with 'sit down in the kingdom', and only he puts the prophets in the list — and the casting out and the children of the kingdom are Matthew's. A composite of the two synoptic forms rather than either one, which is itself the finding.

5:28.text: Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.

provenance.other: “prepare to meet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's form is the passive of it — 'ye are not prepared to meet God' — repeated at 5:29 and 5:31 as a refrain.
provenance.significance: Amos 4:12 is the end of a chapter of withheld judgments: five times God says 'yet have ye not returned unto me', and then, because the warnings failed, 'prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.' It is not an invitation. It is the sentence that follows the exhausting of invitations, and what Israel is being told to prepare for is the meeting itself, on the far side of repentance's last refusal. Alma 5 is built the same way — three times over, at 5:28, 5:29 and 5:31, a hearer is told he is not prepared and that he must prepare quickly — and the borrowed line brings its own deadline with it. The chapter's other refrain, the axe already laid at the root (5:52), is the New Testament version of the same threat, so the sermon is bracketed by the two KJV passages in which the time for warning has just run out.

5:28.note: 'Are ye stripped of pride? I say unto you, if ye are not, ye are not prepared to meet God.' The KJV says 'prepare to meet thy God' once, in Amos, and the Book of Mormon has turned the imperative into a diagnosis: not 'prepare' but 'ye are not prepared', which is why the sentence can be repeated as a test at 5:29 and 5:31. 'Stripped of pride' and 'stripped of envy' are the Book of Mormon's own; the KJV never strips a person of an abstraction.

5:34.text: And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.

provenance.other: “water of life” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Revelation 21:6, 22:1 and 22:17 — and all three are in the last two chapters of Revelation; “bread of life” occurs in exactly two, John 6:35 and 6:48. The Book of Mormon's clause fuses three of Revelation's: the tree of life whose fruit is given to him that overcometh (2:7 and 22:14), the water of life taken 'freely' (22:17, and 21:6 to him that is athirst), and the invitation 'Come'. 'Bread of life' is not Revelation's but John 6:35's; the KJV never puts bread and the water of life in one clause, which is the Book of Mormon's own splice.
provenance.significance: Revelation 22:17 is the last invitation in the Bible and it is issued by the Spirit and the bride — that is, by the church — to whoever will come. Alma 5:33-34 has God issue it himself, 'he sendeth an invitation unto all men', and the sermon ends at 5:62 by making Alma the one who repeats it to those outside the church: 'unto those which do not belong to the church, I speak by way of invitation.' The borrowing therefore carries its speaker with it. The chapter's closing move is to put the preacher in the position Revelation gives the bride, and the fruit of the tree of life is what he offers, which in Revelation 2:7 and 22:14 is reserved for those who overcome and keep the commandments.

5:34.note: 'Come unto me and ye shall partake of the fruit of the tree of life; yea, ye shall eat and drink of the bread and the waters of life freely.' Three of Revelation's images in one sentence, with 'freely' — the word that makes the invitation unconditional — carried over from 22:17 and 21:6. Isaiah 55:1's 'come ye to the waters ... without money and without price' is the Old Testament behind Revelation and may be independently in view; the presence of the tree of life and of 'freely' points at Revelation.

5:37.text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.

provenance.route: Matthew 9:36, with Isaiah 53:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “as sheep having no shepherd” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The related figures are worded differently — Numbers 27:17 and 1 Kings 22:17 have 'as sheep which have no shepherd', Mark 6:34 'as sheep not having a shepherd' — so the Book of Mormon has Matthew's exact participle and word order. 'Gone astray' is Isaiah 53:6's, 'All we like sheep have gone astray'.
provenance.significance: The sentence welds the two halves of the KJV's sheep language and reverses the moral of each. Matthew 9:36's shepherdless crowd moves Jesus to compassion — they are not blamed, they have no shepherd. Isaiah 53:6's straying sheep are blamed, and the verse ends by laying their iniquity on another. Alma 5:37 makes them one accusation and adds the fact that removes the excuse: 'notwithstanding a shepherd hath called after you, and art still calling after you, but ye will not hearken unto his voice.' These sheep have a shepherd. The borrowed phrase is used precisely against itself, and the next two verses name the shepherd from John 10.

5:37.note: 'Ye have gone astray, as sheep having no shepherd.' Matthew 9:36 is the KJV's only instance of the phrase in this exact form, and Isaiah 53:6 supplies the verb. The point of the row is the qualification that follows in the same verse, which cancels the condition the borrowed clause describes.

5:38.text: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

provenance.other: “the good shepherd” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:11 and John 10:14, and nowhere else in the Bible. “one fold” occurs in exactly one, John 10:16. The Book of Mormon uses 'the good shepherd' five times in this chapter alone.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:38-39 does not merely borrow the title; it reproduces the chapter's structure. John 10 runs on the sheep knowing the shepherd's voice (10:3-4), on the good shepherd naming himself (10:11, 10:14), and on there being one fold (10:16) — and Alma asks, in order, whether his hearers hearken to the voice, tells them the good shepherd calls 'in his own name ... which is the name of Christ', and then asks the question John's 'one fold' makes unanswerable: 'if ye are not the sheep of the good shepherd, of what fold are ye?' John leaves one fold and no alternative; Alma supplies the alternative — 'the Devil is your shepherd, and ye are of his fold' — which is a completion of John's figure that John does not offer and that John 10:12's hireling and wolf make possible. The wolf returns at 5:59-60.

5:38.note: 'The good shepherd doth call you; yea, and in his own name he doth call you, which is the name of Christ.' The title exists in the KJV only at John 10:11 and 10:14. What the sermon adds is the second fold: because John allows only one, Alma's question 'of what fold are ye?' has a single available answer and he gives it. Adjudicated at 5:38; the shepherd runs through 5:39, 5:41, 5:57 and 5:60.

5:39.text: Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son.

provenance.route: 1 John 2:22 with Acts 13:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “is a liar” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, three of them in 1 John; only 1 John 2:22 attaches the charge to denying — 'Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ?' “child of the devil” in the singular occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10, Paul's rebuke of Elymas; 1 John 3:10 has the plural.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:39 fuses the two. 'Whosoever denieth this, is a liar and a child of the Devil' takes the denier-is-a-liar of 1 John 2:22 and the singular epithet of Acts 13:10, and lands where 1 John 3:10 already stands: 'In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil.' What is denied has changed, and instructively. In 1 John the lie is denying that Jesus is the Christ; in Alma it is denying Alma's own inference — that a man who is not the good shepherd's sheep must be the Devil's. The borrowed apparatus of antichrist is thereby attached to a conclusion the sermon has just reached rather than to a creed, which is the strongest rhetorical move in the chapter and the one most worth flagging to a reader.

5:39.note: 'Whosoever denieth this, is a liar and a child of the Devil.' The two components have precise KJV homes — the denier-liar of 1 John 2:22 and the singular 'child of the devil' of Acts 13:10 — and are joined nowhere in the Bible. Moderate rather than high because both are short and the vocabulary of liars and devils is available generally; the pairing, and the fact that each half is rare, is the evidence.

5:42.text: For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

provenance.other: “wages of sin” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Wages' by itself occurs in exactly seventeen and is everywhere else a labourer's pay; Romans 6:23 is the only KJV verse in which wages are what sin pays and what is paid is death.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:41-42 has the whole of Romans 6:16-23 compressed: whom you obey you follow, whom you follow you serve, and the servant is paid. Paul's argument turns on the clause Alma 5:42 reproduces almost as a technical term — 'as to things pertaining unto righteousness' answers Romans 6:20's 'when ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness'. The metalepsis is in what Romans 6:23 goes on to say and Alma 5:42 withholds: 'but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.' Paul's sentence has two halves and its force is the asymmetry between them — sin pays a wage, God gives a gift. Alma quotes the first half at the man who has chosen the Devil and lets the second half stand unspoken; it has already been offered, at 5:33-34, to anyone who will come.

5:42.note: 'Whosoever doeth this must receive his wages of him; therefore, for his wages he receiveth death, as to things pertaining unto righteousness, being dead unto all good works.' The KJV pays a wage for sin exactly once. The Book of Mormon keeps Paul's transaction and his righteousness clause and drops his contrast, which is the interpretive fact worth recording.

5:48.text: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

provenance.route: John 1:14 and 1:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “only begotten of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “full of grace and truth” occurs in exactly one — the same verse, John 1:14, where they stand in the same order and adjacent. The Book of Mormon inserts one word into the second: 'full of grace, and mercy, and truth'.
provenance.significance: The inserted 'mercy' is the whole interest of the row. John 1:14's pair is fixed KJV vocabulary and is repeated at 1:17, and the triad grace-mercy-truth exists in the KJV only in epistolary greetings (1 Timothy 1:2, 2 Timothy 1:2, 2 John 1:3), never of the incarnate Word. Behind those greetings stands Exodus 34:6's 'abundant in goodness and truth', the formula John is widely taken to be rewriting. So the Book of Mormon's version reads as John 1:14 with a term restored from the Old Testament formula John compressed. The verse then adds John 1:29 — 'it is he that cometh to take away the sins of the world' against 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' — with the singular sin pluralised and the Lamb dropped, so that the second borrowing is de-Johannine in exactly the way the first is not.
provenance.alternative: If the triad is taken from an epistolary greeting rather than from John, the source is 2 John 1:3 or 1 Timothy 1:2; but neither has 'the only begotten of the Father' beside it, and that phrase is a KJV singleton.

5:48.note: 'The Son of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace, and mercy, and truth. And behold, it is he that cometh to take away the sins of the world.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, in order, with one word interpolated — this is a quotation on any definition, though it is below Skousen's threshold and is not one of his 36. Frederick's monograph is an argument about the Gospel of John in the Book of Mormon and his discussion of John 1:12-14 falls in the same passage of his book as this verse; the catalogue's index of him records that co-occurrence and nothing stronger, and no claim about what he identifies is made here.

5:50.text: To the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen.

provenance.route: Jude 1:25 and Psalm 47:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “majesty dominion and power” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jude 1:25, where the full series is 'glory and majesty, dominion and power' — four nouns that Alma 5:50 has in 'his glory, in his might, majesty, power and dominion', with 'might' added and the last two reversed. “King of all the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 47:7.
provenance.significance: Both borrowings are doxological and both are moved. Jude's four nouns are the closing ascription of an epistle, said to God; Alma 5:50 makes them the equipage of an arrival — 'the Son of God cometh in his glory, in his might, majesty, power and dominion'. Psalm 47:7's title belongs to a psalm of enthronement sung after a victory, and Alma applies it to a king who has not yet appeared: 'Behold the glory of the King of all the earth; and also the King of Heaven shall very soon shine forth.' A doxology for what God is has become a description of what is about to happen, which is the tense the whole sermon is written in.

5:50.note: 'The Son of God cometh in his glory, in his might, majesty, power and dominion ... Behold the glory of the King of all the earth.' Two KJV singletons in one verse, neither reproduced as a clause: Jude's four-noun ascription with a fifth interpolated, and Psalm 47:7's royal title. Recorded as an echo because the agreement is a vocabulary set rather than a construction; the case is that both sets are unique in the KJV and both are in the same sentence.
5:50.whyNot: Doxological nouns cluster in the KJV and a writer working in that register could reassemble them without a source; 1 Peter 5:11, Revelation 1:6 and Revelation 5:13 all have overlapping series. The claim rests on Jude 1:25 being the only verse with these three in sequence, and on the coincidence with the Psalm 47 title in the same breath.

5:52.text: And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.other: “the axe is laid” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9, which are the same sentence in the two Gospels; “hewn down and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three, those two and Matthew 7:19. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Matthew 3:10 against Luke 3:9 and reported no decisive divergence, because the two differ only in the position of 'therefore', which its matcher ignores as a common word. The judgment is therefore made by eye, on two points. First, word order: Matthew 3:10 reads 'therefore every tree which', Luke 3:9 'every tree therefore which', and the Book of Mormon reads 'therefore every tree that' — Matthew's order, though the relative pronoun is neither Gospel's here but Matthew 7:19's, whose sentence is 'Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire' and which the machine ranked above both Baptist verses. Second, and decisively, the same verse ends 'even an unquenchable fire': “unquenchable fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:12, while Luke 3:17 has the inverted “fire unquenchable”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse of its own. The chapter's repeated 'kingdom of Heaven' (5:28, 5:50, 5:51) points the same way, since Luke never uses the phrase.
provenance.significance: John the Baptist's preaching is the armature of the entire sermon, not a single citation. Matthew 3:2's 'Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand' is Alma 5:28, 5:50 and 5:51; Matthew 3:8's 'fruits meet for repentance' is Alma 5:54's 'works which is meet for repentance'; Matthew 3:10's axe and burning are Alma 5:35, 5:36, 5:52 and 5:56; Matthew 3:12's unquenchable fire closes 5:52. The metalepsis is in who is being addressed. In Matthew, John says all of it to Pharisees and Sadducees who have come out to his baptism — insiders presenting themselves for a rite — and warns them not to plead descent from Abraham. Alma 5 is preached to the members of a church, is preoccupied from 5:24 with whether they may sit down with Abraham, and ends at 5:62 by inviting the outsiders to be baptized. The sermon has been built on the one New Testament passage where the baptizer's threat falls on the people already inside.

5:52.note: 'Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the tree; therefore every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be hewn down and cast into the fire; yea, a fire which cannot be consumed; even an unquenchable fire.' A near-verbatim reproduction of Matthew 3:10 with Matthew 3:12's closing phrase appended. Attributed within the sermon to the Spirit — 'the spirit saith' — and closed with 'the holy one hath spoken it', which is worth noting: the Book of Mormon assigns the Baptist's words to their speaker's source rather than to the Baptist.

5:53.text: Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?

provenance.other: “trodden under foot the Son of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Trodden under foot' by itself occurs in five and was set aside as common vocabulary at Alma 4:2; what makes this instance different is that the object is a person, which the KJV has only here.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 10:29 is the KJV's severest sentence about apostasy, and every element of it is already in this sermon. It asks what punishment is due to one who 'hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing' — trampling, blood, sanctification, holiness. Alma 5:53-54 has the trampling of the holy one, and one verse later the hearers' brethren 'have been sanctified by the holy spirit'; the blood of the covenant is the blood that has been washing garments since 5:21. And Hebrews 10:26's premise — 'if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth' — is the situation of Alma 5 exactly: a church, having known, persisting. The borrowing brings the harshest available frame to bear on people who are still being invited to repent.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 7:6's swine that 'trample them under their feet' is the other KJV trampling of something holy, and 'the holy' is its object there too ('give not that which is holy unto the dogs'); it is arguably nearer in wording and further in argument.

5:53.note: 'Can ye lay aside these things, and trample the holy one under your feet.' The KJV tramples a divine person once, at Hebrews 10:29, and the surrounding verses supply the blood, the sanctifying and the wilful sin that the rest of Alma 5:53-54 is made of. Moderate rather than high because the Book of Mormon's verb is 'trample' and the KJV's is 'trodden'; Matthew 7:6 has 'trample' with a holy object and is kept as the alternative.

5:57.text: Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you.

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:11 → 2 Corinthians 6:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Isaiah 52:11 in the KJV reads 'Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD.'
provenance.other: “be ye separate” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “touch not the unclean” occurs in exactly one — both 2 Corinthians 6:17, and neither is in Isaiah. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Alma 5:57 against Isaiah 52:11 and 2 Corinthians 6:17 and returns one decisive point, for Paul: the Book of Mormon has 'among them, and be ye separate' where Isaiah has 'thence'. Paul's negative is 'touch not the unclean thing' and Isaiah's is 'touch no unclean thing'; Alma 5:57 has 'touch not their unclean things', which is Paul's construction with the noun made plural and possessive.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest mediation result in the chapter and it is worth stating plainly: where the Book of Mormon quotes an Old Testament verse that the New Testament also quotes, this verse follows the New Testament's wording, including the clause Paul added and Isaiah does not contain. Recovering Paul's context then does real work. 2 Corinthians 6:17 is the centre of a paragraph about being unequally yoked with unbelievers, addressed to a congregation and demanding separation inside a mixed community — not the exodus from Babylon that Isaiah 52:11 describes. Alma 5:57 needs exactly Paul's situation and not Isaiah's: his hearers are not in exile among foreigners, they are a church with wicked members in it, and the separation he commands is a purging of a name-list, not a journey. The verse that follows in Paul, 'I will receive you', is also already in this sermon, at 5:33.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 52:11 is the ultimate source and is quoted elsewhere in the Book of Mormon (3 Nephi 20:41); the mediation call here is about which English wording Alma 5:57 has, not about which text is older.

5:57.note: 'Come ye out from the wicked, and be ye separate, and touch not their unclean things.' Against 2 Corinthians 6:17: 'Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing.' Three clauses in order, with 'from among them' replaced by 'from the wicked' — which is the only substantive change and is a gloss, naming who 'them' are. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his 36; catalogued as a quotation on the reproduction of the clauses.

5:57.text: Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.

provenance.other: “blotted out of the book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “written with the righteous” occurs in exactly one — the same verse, Psalm 69:28, and in that order. 'Book of life' by itself occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, six of them in Revelation, so the book is common property and the pairing of the blotting with the not-being-written-among-the-righteous is not.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:57-58 has all three of Psalm 69:28's moves and keeps them in the psalm's sequence: the names blotted out, the names of the wicked not numbered among the names of the righteous, and then the names of the righteous written in the book of life. The KJV's one verse that does the same work is the psalmist's imprecation against his persecutors. What the Book of Mormon changes is the agent and the mood. In the psalm the blotting is asked of God against enemies; in Alma it is an administrative consequence of a separation the hearers perform themselves — 'come ye out from the wicked ... and behold, their names shall be blotted out'. A curse has become a church register. Revelation 3:5's promise, that the overcomer's name will not be blotted out of the book of life, is the New Testament form and is the verse that supplies the white raiment this sermon has been using since 5:21; both halves of Revelation 3:5 are in Alma 5, which is worth recording even though the wording here is the psalm's.

5:57.note: 'Their names shall be blotted out, that the names of the wicked shall not be numbered among the names of the righteous ... For the names of the righteous shall be written in the Book of Life.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, in order. Alma 5:57 then attributes the sentence to scripture — 'that the word of God may be fulfilled, which saith, The names of the wicked shall not be mingled with the names of my people' — and the words quoted are in no KJV verse; the nearest thing the KJV has to the citation being claimed is Psalm 69:28, which is the link.

5:60.text: For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.

provenance.other: “enter in among you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is the KJV's only wolves entering a flock: 'after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.' “ravening wolves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:15, which is the adjective behind the Book of Mormon's 'ravenous wolf'. John 10:12's wolf catches and scatters but does not enter.
provenance.significance: Acts 20 is Paul's farewell to the elders of Ephesus, and the verse before the wolves is the one that makes the borrowing pointed: 'Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God.' It is a charge to pastors about what will happen when the pastor leaves. Alma 5:59-60 turns it into a charge to the flock itself — 'he commandeth you that ye suffer no ravenous wolf to enter among you' — so the duty of the overseer is devolved onto the congregation, which is precisely the move Alma 4:18-20 made when he kept the priesthood and asked the people to be watched over by a word rather than an office. The chapter's shepherd language began at 5:38 with John 10 and ends here with Acts 20, and between them the shepherd has stopped being only Christ.

5:60.note: 'He commandeth you that ye suffer no ravenous wolf to enter among you, that ye may not be destroyed.' Acts 20:29 is the KJV's only verse with wolves entering in among a flock and the only verse with the phrase 'enter in among you'; Matthew 7:15 supplies 'ravening', which the Book of Mormon has as 'ravenous'. The previous verse's rhetorical question — 'what shepherd is there among you having many sheep, doth not watch over them, that the wolves enter not and devour his flock?' — states the same figure first and is covered by this row.
